name: Jesse White
description: Born 1934 in Alton, Illinois; Alabama State College graduate (1957, two-sport athlete); U.S. Army paratrooper (101st Airborne); minor-league baseball in the Chicago Cubs farm system; 33-year Chicago Public Schools teacher and administrator. Founded the Jesse White Tumbling Team in 1959 for children in and around Chicago public housing (18,500+ alumni). Elected to the Illinois General Assembly in 1974 (16 years); Cook County Recorder of Deeds 1992-1998; elected Illinois Secretary of State in 1998 - the first African American to hold the office and the longest-serving in state history (six terms). Retired at the end of his sixth term; the state office building at 115 S. LaSalle St., Chicago was renamed the 'Jesse White State of Illinois Building' in his honor in 2025.

description: RCA Victor's Chicago recording studios (Studios 1, 2, and 3). Three locations: c.1927-1935 at 952 N. Michigan Avenue; 1935-April 1969 at 445 N. name: Imports Etc.
description: Legendary Chicago record store and hub for house DJs. name: Gramaphone Records
description: DJ-based vinyl record store at 2843 N. Clark Street, Chicago — one of the legendary incubators of Chicago house music. Opened in 1969 selling folk, jazz, and blues; by the 1980s it was selling house music records, the first Chicago-area store of its kind focusing on vinyl for DJs, and a destination for traveling DJs. description: Controversial Black weekly newspaper founded by Julius F. Taylor: first issued August 31, 1895 in Salt Lake City, Utah, and moved to Chicago in 1899 after conflicts with the Latter Day Saints. name: Associated Negro Press
description: The first national news wire service for African-American newspapers: founded in Chicago on March 2, 1919, by Claude Albert Barnett and headquartered at 312 S. Clark Street. With correspondents in every major center of Black population — the first African American news-gathering service with African American foreign correspondents — the ANP supplied news, columns, features and reviews to about 150 U.S. Black newspapers and 100 African papers (in French and English), reaching ~200 papers worldwide at its early-1950s peak. Bankrolled by Barnett's Kashmir Chemical Company; ceased operation in 1964 (a 1967 end-date account is recorded as conflict CTL-CFL-000250).

name: Lil Hardin Armstrong
description: Jazz pianist, composer, bandleader, and arranger (b. Lillian Beatrice Hardin, Memphis, February 3, 1898; d. Chicago, August 27, 1971). Pianist and arranger of King Oliver’s Creole Jazz Band in Chicago (1921–24); married fellow band member Louis Armstrong (February 5, 1924; divorced 1938), taught him to read music, and urged him to go solo; pianist and recording artist on Armstrong’s Hot Five sessions (1925–28); composed "Struttin’ with Some Barbeque." name: Earl 'Fatha' Hines
description: Jazz pianist Earl Kenneth "Fatha" Hines (b. Duquesne, Pennsylvania, December 28, 1903; d. Oakland, April 22, 1983). Classical piano lessons from age nine; recording debut 1923 with vocalist Lois Deppe; moved to Chicago in 1925. Met Louis Armstrong at Chicago’s Musicians’ Union (State & 39th); musical director of Armstrong’s Stompers (Sunset Café, 1927); recorded nineteen historic sides with Armstrong’s Hot Five/Hot Seven (1927–28), including "West End Blues" and the duet "Weather Bird." Opened at Chicago’s Grand Terrace Café on December 28, 1928, leading his own big band — led the orchestra until 1948; his 1943 band featured Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Sarah Vaughan, and Billy Eckstine. Sideman in the Louis Armstrong All-Stars (1948–51); 1964 Little Theater comeback; tombstone reads "Piano Man."

name: Johnny Griffin
description: Chicago-born hard-bop tenor saxophonist (1928–2008) known as the "Little Giant." Created the Thomas Associates record-promotion business in the mid-1970s (clients: Ray Charles, Barry White, Quincy Jones, the Stylistics, Johnny Taylor); shepherded The Independents ('Leaving Me' sold 1M+); acclaimed poet. First issued November 1989 as a 20-page photocopied zine from Ford's Chicago apartment under the tagline “She Knows Who She Is,” it documented ball, club, and house culture, platformed pioneers such as Frankie Knuckles, Larry Heard, Deee-Lite, and RuPaul, and carried uncompromising HIV/AIDS coverage. Publication ended with Ford's death in 1993; a 460-page anthology of all ten issues was released by Primary Information in February 2025.

name: House jacking / house-dance community
description: Jacking — the freestyle torso-rippling dance move — emerged within Chicago house music in the 1980s, with Warehouse, Power Plant, and Music Box connections. It is the most famous dance move associated with early house music and, with footwork and lofting, one of the three main elements of house dance. The jack left its trace in record titles from Chip E.'s 'Jack Trax' EP (1985) to Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk's 'Jack'n the House' (1985) and Steve 'Silk' Hurley's 'Jack Your Body' (1986). House dance is associated with complete freedom of expression and draws on waacking, voguing, capoeira, jazz dance, Lindy Hop, tap, and modern dance.

name: Black queer house dance-floor community
description: The founding dance floor of Chicago house was Black and Latinx and queer. At the Warehouse — opened 1977 at 206 S. Jefferson St. by promoter Robert Williams with Frankie Knuckles as resident DJ (1977–1982) — a members-only nonprofit juice bar gave Chicago's Black gay community dancefloor freedom; Black and Latinx LGBTQ men and women found community, hope, acceptance and transcendence in Knuckles' music. The city's landmark report sets the period of significance at 1977–1982; on June 21, 2023, the City Council designated the Warehouse a Chicago Landmark as a safe haven for LGBTQ+ communities. This community is represented in the graph primarily through the Warehouse venue node and THING publication node; this node exists to name the people-network as its own entity.

name: Roller-rink dance community
description: Chicago's Black roller rinks were dance floors in their own right -- skating venues where R&B, soul, and early house played and where skate-dance styles developed. Anchor venue The Rink was founded in 1975 by Carmen Clark and Nate Simpson at 8920 S Ashland Ave, moving in 1983 to 1122 E 87th St, where it remains. Spinning R&B 45s with a DJ (rather than a Wurlitzer organist) inspired "JB skating," a style rooted in James Brown's dancing -- crisscross footwork, dips, spins -- born on the South Side and since spread nationally. The rink circuit connected the disco-to-house transition for skaters who never entered the clubs, extending the dance floor's geography.

name: Jesse B. Blayton Sr.
description: Atlanta accountant, banker, and broadcast pioneer: born December 6, 1897 in Fallis, Oklahoma; studied at the Walton School of Chicago and the University of Chicago before moving to Atlanta in 1922. Became Georgia's first Black Certified Public Accountant in 1928 (fourth African American nationwide); taught accounting at Atlanta University; was founding president of Mutual Federal Savings and Loan Association (1925-1971). In 1949 he bought 1,000-watt station WERD for $50,000, becoming the first African American to own and operate a radio station in the United States; WERD pioneered 'Negro appeal' programming for the local Black audience, and in the 1960s shared quarters with the SCLC. Sold WERD in 1968; died September 7, 1977; inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 1995.

name: Percy Sutton
description: Percy Ellis Sutton (1920-2009): civil rights attorney, politician, and media-ownership pioneer. Youngest of 15 children of a former slave's family; born in San Antonio, Texas; served in WWII with the Tuskegee Airmen as an intelligence officer (captain). Law degree 1950; opened a Harlem law office with his brother Oliver in 1953 and represented Malcolm X. Served in the New York State Assembly; member of Harlem's 'Gang of Four.' Manhattan borough president 1966-1977 (21st; September 13, 1966 to December 31, 1977) - the longest tenure, and the highest-ranking African American elected official in New York City. Led the group that founded Inner City Broadcasting (see conflict CTL-CFL-002446); bought WLIB-AM in 1972 for $1.9 million (first Black-owned NYC station); bought the Apollo Theater for $250,000 in 1981. Received the NAACP Spingarn Medal in 1987; an East Harlem park was named in his honor in 2021. Died December 26, 2009.

description: (2019-04 to 2019-07) Johnson Publishing Company filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy protection on April 9, 2019. Simmons is an Emmy Award-winning cinematographer and UCLA professor of cinematography.

name: Irene McCoy Gaines
description: Social worker, clubwoman, and political organizer (1892-1964). Born in Florida, raised in Chicago; studied social work at Fisk University and the University of Chicago. Stenographer at Cook County Juvenile Court; 1917 director of the Girls' Work Division (War Camp Community Service); industrial secretary of the first Black YWCA branch; Chicago Urban League leader; Cook County Welfare Department social worker for 15 years from 1930. Founded the Chicago Council of Negro Organizations (1939; president 1939-1953, ~100 member orgs); led the 1941 Washington lobbying trip preceding Executive Order 8802; appointed to Hoover's National Committee on Negro Housing (1931), leading to the Ida B. Wells Homes. First Black woman to run for the Illinois legislature (1940); 15th president of the National Association of Colored Women's Clubs (1952-1958); testified at the UN (1947). Died of cancer 1964-04-07. CHA's 151-unit Irene McCoy Gaines Apartments (East Garfield Park) bear her name.

name: Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32 (1940)

name: Hyde Park Township
description: Former civil township in Cook County, Illinois — a separate municipality from 1861 until its annexation into Chicago in 1889. Created by the Illinois General Assembly in 1861, it stretched from Pershing Road (39th Street) to 138th Street and the Calumet River, State Street to Lake Michigan and the Indiana state line — much of what is now Chicago's South Side. In the June 29, 1889 elections the township's voters (population ~85,000) approved annexation. After annexation the 'Hyde Park' neighborhood name narrowed to the historic core between 51st and 55th Streets near the lakefront.

name: HOLC redlining — 63rd Street corridor (areas incl. D74)
description: HOLC graded large parts of Chicago's South Side, including the Black Belt, D ('hazardous'). Area D74 ran from 35th to 67th Street between State Street and Cottage Grove — the heart of the Black Belt, including Bronzeville and Washington Park. Its area description discusses restricting 'the colored people' via real-estate protective associations and cites Washington Park as 'almost completely monopolized by the colored race' as rationale for the grade; it also flags the Ida B. Wells housing project for 'unsettling patterns of tradition.' Public housing built in Chicago from the 1930s to the 1960s was largely located in HOLC 'hazardous' neighborhoods.

name: Parkway Gardens
description: Parkway Gardens (Parkway Garden Homes): 694-unit affordable-housing complex of 35 buildings on 13 acres at 6330-6546 S. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive, Chicago (Greater Grand Crossing, bordering Woodlawn and Washington Park). Built 1950-1955 by architect Henry K. name: Elijah McCoy
description: Canadian-American inventor (May 2, 1844-October 10, 1929) whose automatic steam-engine lubricator gave rise to the phrase 'the real McCoy.' Son of George and Mildred McCoy, who escaped Kentucky slavery via the Underground Railroad to Colchester, Ontario; apprenticed in mechanical engineering at the University of Edinburgh as a teenager. Denied engineering work by racism, he worked as a locomotive fireman and oiler on the Michigan Central Railroad, then invented the automatic lubricator (patented 1872); by 1900 it was on almost all North American railroads. Held 57+ patents, including a 1916 graphite lubricator; founded the Elijah McCoy Manufacturing Company in 1920.

name: Mary Jackson
description: Mary Winston Jackson (April 9, 1921 - February 11, 2005): mathematician and aerospace engineer. B.S. in mathematics and physical science, Hampton Institute (1942). Joined NACA's Langley laboratory in 1951 as a 'computer' in the segregated West Area Computing division under supervisor Dorothy Vaughan. Moved to the 4-by-4-foot Supersonic Pressure Tunnel under engineer Kazimierz Czarnecki; after completing graduate-level courses at segregated Hampton High School (with special permission), she became NASA's first Black female engineer in 1958. Authored or co-authored nearly a dozen research reports on boundary-layer airflow. In 1979 she accepted a demotion to manage Langley's Federal Women's Program and Affirmative Action Program, advancing women in STEM. Retired 1985 after 34 years. One of three protagonists of Hidden Figures (book and 2016 film). Posthumous Congressional Gold Medal (2019); NASA's Washington, D.C. headquarters renamed the Mary W. Jackson NASA Headquarters.

name: Patricia E. Bath
description: Patricia Era Bath (1942-2019): Harlem-born ophthalmologist, laser scientist, inventor, and humanitarian. First African American to complete an ophthalmology residency (NYU, 1970-1973); first woman ophthalmologist on the UCLA medical school faculty (Jules Stein Eye Institute, 1974); co-founded the American Institute for the Prevention of Blindness (1976) and pioneered community ophthalmology. First woman to head a U.S. ophthalmology residency program (King-Drew-UCLA, 1983). Inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2022 (among the first Black women inductees). Died May 30, 2019, in San Francisco.

name: Percy Lavon Julian
description: Percy Lavon Julian (1899-1975): research chemist and pioneer in the chemical synthesis of medicinal drugs from plants. Born in Montgomery, Alabama, the grandson of slaves; first in his family to attend college (DePauw B.A. 1920; Harvard M.S. 1923; Vienna Ph.D. 1931). First to synthesize physostigmine, the glaucoma drug (1935). Denied faculty posts, he spent 18 years as Glidden's director of research (Soya Products Division), developing soy-protein fire-fighting foam used by the Navy in WWII and intermediates for synthetic progesterone, testosterone, and cortisone. Left Glidden in 1953; established Julian Laboratories (sold 1961, making him one of the first Black millionaires); founded the nonprofit Julian Research Institute (1964). First African American chemist elected to the National Academy of Sciences (1973). Held over 130 patents. Died of liver cancer in Waukegan, Illinois, April 19, 1975. PBS NOVA's 'Forgotten Genius'; USPS commemorative stamp, 1993.

name: Pullman sleeping car porters
description: Black railroad service workers employed by the Chicago-based Pullman Company to prepare, maintain, and operate sleeping cars across the U.S. rail network, c. 1870-1968. The Pullman Palace Car Company (est. 1867; Pullman Company from 1900) was the largest employer of African Americans -- some 12,000 Black workers by the 1920s -- while barring them from conductor jobs and paying porters low wages for long hours. On August 25, 1925 the porters organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters under A. Philip Randolph, the first predominantly Black labor union; after a twelve-year struggle it won the first collective bargaining agreement ever secured by a Black union (1937).

name: JPC Photo Archive (NMAAHC + Getty)
description: Ebony/Jet photographic archive of the Johnson Publishing Company: 3.35M negatives and slides, 983,000 photographs, 166,000 contact sheets, 9,000 audio/visual recordings - the most significant collection illustrating African American life in the 20th century (WWII through the civil rights movement and the 1980s-90s culture boom). Acquired for $30M by the Ford, J. name: Joseph Harrison Jackson
description: Baptist minister (September 11, 1900 - August 18, 1990), born near Rudyard, Mississippi; B.A. Jackson College (1926), B.D. Colgate Rochester Divinity School (1932), M.A. Creighton University (1934); ordained at 22, pastor of First Baptist Church, McComb, Mississippi. Often clashed with Martin Luther King Jr., opposing the use of civil disobedience in the civil rights movement. Charter member of the World Council of Churches (1937, 1948 planning conferences); vice president of the Baptist World Alliance.

description: Historically Black Masonic fraternity founded by Boston abolitionist Prince Hall. In Illinois, North Star Lodge was organized in Chicago in 1852 (Ohio jurisdiction); with lodges in Alton (1856) and Springfield (1857) it formed the Prince Hall Grand Lodge for the State of Illinois in 1867. name: Kenneth Morris
description: African American gospel composer and publisher (1917–1989). Born August 28, 1917, in Jamaica, New York; began as a professional jazz musician, studied at the Manhattan Conservatory of Music, and relocated permanently to Chicago after falling ill while performing at the 1934 Chicago World's Fair. Organist and choir director at First Church of Deliverance (1937), where he introduced the Hammond organ to gospel music. Co-founded Martin and Morris Music Company with Sallie Martin (1940) — the nation's oldest continuously running Black gospel publishing company (1940–1989). Arranged and published the first widely-known "Just a Closer Walk with Thee" (1940); composed "Yes, God Is Real," "Christ Is All," "King Jesus Will Roll All Your Burdens Away," and "Dig a Little Deeper in God's Love."

name: House music — name origin
description: The contested origin of the genre name 'house music': the consensus derivation is from the Warehouse nightclub at 206 S. name: Appomattox Club
description: Elite Black social and civic club of Chicago, organized circa 1900 in connection with Edward Wright as “black Chicago's version of the Commercial Club.” Named for the Virginia courthouse where the Civil War effectively ended, it was a political and social powerhouse where Black business and political leaders gathered to talk policy and influence elections. From 1920 it occupied a three-story stone mansion at 3632 Grand Boulevard / South Parkway (now Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive; building no longer stands); the address served as headquarters for the 1940 American Negro Exposition planning. Described in the Congressional Record as one of the first African American political organizations in the country. Closed in the late 1960s.

name: Black Independent Political Organization (BIPO)
description: Independent Black political organization for voter education and mobilization, deliberately separate from both the Daley machine and the official Washington campaign. Its steering committee was formed December 13, 1982 (62 members, 71% Black), led by Bill Berry (Johnson Products), Warren Bacon (Inland Steel), and Walter Clark (First Federal Saving and Loan), to provide policy/planning and develop financial and political resources for Harold Washington's 1983 mayoral campaign — which Washington won in April 1983 with 50.06% of the vote and 98% of the Black vote.

name: Black Ward Democratic Organizations (Dawson-era Machine)
description: Patronage-for-votes machine: precinct captains and ward committeemen traded city/county jobs and services for disciplined Black voter turnout delivered to the Daley Democratic machine. Dawson mentored Ralph Metcalfe; both men were later enlisted by Daley as emissaries to the Black community.

name: Chicago Black United Communities (CBUC)
description: Black political education and voter-mobilization infrastructure on Chicago's South Side. Founded circa 1980 by Lu Palmer and Jorja Palmer as a nonprofit; began as a coalition of local Black groups and became a membership organization training Black Chicagoans in electoral politics. Ran political education classes modeled on the Black Panther Party's programs under Fred Hampton, in four-week cycles with graduations at which Harold Washington spoke. Trained and deployed some 2,000 organizers; worked with the Urban League, NAACP, and Operation PUSH to register 237,000 new voters (180,000 Black) and raised a near-half-million-dollar war chest, building the constituency that elected Harold Washington mayor in 1983.

name: Overcrowded segregated schooling (double shifts)
description: Chicago's Black Belt schools running double (two four-hour) shifts per day to handle enrollment surges from the Great Migration, with vocational tracking and stark resource gaps versus white schools. Between 1930 and 1940 the combined enrollment of 24 Bronzeville schools rose 65%; the district answered with 'doubleshift' schedules - Black students attended only part of the day - to preserve segregation. Superintendent Benjamin Willis (1953-1966) added 'Willis Wagons' portable trailers for Black students rather than sending them to under-capacity white schools. Over 200,000 students walked out in the 1963 Chicago school boycott over these conditions.

name: Homegoing service
description: The African-American Christian funeral tradition framing death as a celebratory 'going home' to the Lord — gospel music, elaborate printed programs, open casket, expressive grief, and the repast — rooted in enslavement-era hush harbors where the enslaved fused African tradition with Christianity in secret, and in the Black church. Homegoings also became explicitly political, from Emmett Till's open-casket funeral to movement funerals, and an economic engine: Black funeral directors became major Reconstruction-era business figures.

name: Easter best and church-hat fashion
description: Easter Sunday as the peak of Black church fashion - 'the Olympics of church fashion': new coordinated outfits for the whole family, elaborate hats ('crowns') for church mothers, children's Easter speeches and programs, and Easter dinner after service. name: Hall Branch Library and Vivian Harsh Collection
description: Bronzeville branch of the Chicago Public Library where Vivian G. Harsh — the first African American to run a CPL branch — built the 'Special Negro Collection' from 1932, modeled on the Schomburg Center, Fisk University Library, and Atlanta University Library collections. With children's librarian Charlemae Hill Rollins (first at the branch, thirty years of service), the collection became an engine of the Chicago Renaissance, drawing support from Richard Wright, Margaret Walker, Arna Bontemps, Gwendolyn Brooks, Langston Hughes, and Horace Cayton. Neglected for a decade after Harsh's 1958 retirement, it was revived by an $89,000 federal grant in 1970 with a full-time curator, renamed the Vivian G. Harsh Collection of Afro-American History and Literature, and moved to the Carter G. Woodson Regional Library in 1975 — today the oldest and largest African American studies repository in the Midwest.

name: Mail-order catalog (Sears / Montgomery Ward)
description: The Sears, Roebuck and Montgomery Ward mail-order catalogs ('Wish Books'): the mass-market catalogs that let Black Southerners order goods anonymously by post, bypassing Jim Crow storefronts. Montgomery Ward issued the first mail-order catalog in 1872; Sears built its empire on the catalog. Because ordering by mail concealed the customer's race, Sears 'had almost no idea which of its customers were black and which were white' and shipped to anyone who could pay. Threatened Southern merchants spread rumors that both companies were Black-owned, held weekend catalog 'book burnings' with $50 bounties, and prompted Sears to publish founders' photos to prove they were white (Ward offered a $100 reward for the rumor's source). Sears kit homes also let Black families bypass sellers who refused to sell to non-whites. Julius Rosenwald, Sears part-owner from 1895, donated $4.3M for nearly 5,000 Rosenwald schools across the rural South (1912-1932). Sears ended its general catalog in 1993.

name: Rev. Dr. Charlie E. Dates
description: Senior pastor of Salem Baptist Church of Chicago (since January 2023) and Progressive Baptist Church of Chicago (since 2011); PhD in Historical Theology from Trinity Evangelical Divinity School; founder of the Spend in the Black Commerce Corridor initiative, the Progressive Center for Counseling & Justice, and the Black Boy Literacy Campaign.

description: Faith-led economic initiative founded by Rev. Dr. Charlie E. Dates and Salem Baptist Church of Chicago (launched 2025) organizing large-scale marketplaces of 100+ Black-owned businesses along 75th Street on the South Side, framed as a long-term strategy for generational wealth.

name: Jazz Showcase
description: Chicago's oldest jazz club (founded 1947 by Joe Segal); 170-seat listening room at 806 S Plymouth Ct (Joe Segal Way), South Loop, in rebuilt Dearborn Station since 2008. Live seven nights a week. Not Black-owned (Segal family); stage, archive, and audience history inseparable from Black artistry.

sources.citation: CultureTechLens, "Venue Scout: Jazz Showcase & Chess Records / Blues Heaven Foundation," October 8, 2026 (CTL strategy file).
jazzshowcase.com (club website; calendar, tickets, private events)

name: Blues Heaven Foundation
description: 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded by Willie Dixon; based at 2120 S Michigan Ave, Chicago (the former Chess Records headquarters/studio building, bought by Marie Dixon in 1993, reopened 1997). Mission: help young musicians with the business of music and provide emergency financial assistance to senior musicians with medical issues. Runs tours, youth programs, and the Blues Garden summer concert series.

sources.citation: CultureTechLens, "Venue Scout: Jazz Showcase & Chess Records / Blues Heaven Foundation," October 8, 2026 (CTL strategy file).
Blues Heaven Foundation (info@BluesHeaven.com; (312) 808-1286)

name: Joe Segal
description: Founder of the Jazz Showcase (1947); NEA Jazz Master who ran the club for nearly 70 years, greeting audiences at the door and taking the cover charge himself. Recorded club performances from the soundboard with musicians' consent across decades, building a contender for the most extensive live jazz archive of its kind. Died 2016; South Plymouth Court renamed Joe Segal Way in his honor. Club now owned/operated by his son Wayne Segal.

sources.citation: CultureTechLens, "Venue Scout: Jazz Showcase & Chess Records / Blues Heaven Foundation," October 8, 2026 (CTL strategy file).
